rows: 68 places · the signature of San Francisco

rows.w: Third-generation cart dim sum since 1958 and a Michelin Bib Gourmand — the Guide calls it 'arguably the place in town for dim sum.' The Shanghai Kurobuta pork dumplings and shrimp har gow are the draws.

Val Cantu's SoMa tasting-menu room — the world's first three-Michelin-star Mexican restaurant — fusing regional technique with Bay Area produce; squab tacos on house sourdough tortillas and a blue-masa Dungeness-crab tostada. Elevated to three Michelin stars in the 2026 California guide (sfist, 2026-06-25).

The Michelin-recognized successor to the beloved Hong Kong Lounge II (which burned down in 2019), reborn in SoMa. Handmade Hong Kong-style dim sum — the crab-and-broth Shanghai dumplings and braised pork belly stand out.
Always-packed SoMa dumpling bar — xiao long bao, har gow and crisp potstickers in a lively room near CCA.
The Bay Area bakery that led the artisan-bread revival — crackly sourdough baguettes and levain loaves at its Ferry Building stall.
MICHELIN-listed Cantonese at Embarcadero Center, by the Ferry Building.
Food-truck-born Filipino-Mexican counter — the pork-sisig burrito is its signature.
All-organic, wood-fired bagels with cult status — crunchy outside, chewy and malty within; house-cultured cream cheese.
Opened 1920 down a Chinatown alley off Sacramento St — widely billed as the oldest dim sum restaurant in the US.
Ex-Hakkasan chef Ho Chee Boon's Cantonese tasting room in the old Empress of China, with Coit Tower views — Peking duck and dim sum courses; MICHELIN-listed.

Chef Brandon Jew's Cal-Chinese landmark in the old Four Families banquet hall — the first Chinatown restaurant to win a Michelin star (2017, held through 2026). Order the honey-butter scallion milk bread and the Peking duck with whipped duck-liver mousse.
The original SF sourdough — same mother starter since 1849, the city's oldest continuously operating business. Get the clam chowder in a sourdough bread bowl.

rows: 148 places · the top tier, graded within each area

rows.w: 1932 Beaux-Arts opera house — home of San Francisco Opera and SF Ballet, and where the UN Charter was signed in 1945.
Award-winning Union Square bar led by local legend Kevin Diedrich; Asian-Pacific-driven drinks that landed it at #16 on North America's 50 Best Bars.
Nite Yun's Cambodian counter in the Ferry Building (successor to Oakland's Nyum Bai) — kuy teav noodle soup and Cambodian fried chicken; Yun a 2025 James Beard Best Chef: California semifinalist.

The world's last manually operated cable-car system, running since 1873; the Powell-Hyde and Powell-Mason lines climb Nob and Russian hills from the Powell/Market turnaround down to Fisherman's Wharf.
The 1898 Beaux-Arts ferry terminal with its landmark clock tower, reborn as a food hall of local artisans; the Tuesday/Thursday/Saturday farmers' market on the plaza is one of the country's best.

rows.w: SF's tallest and most recognizable tower (1972), reopened in 2024 after a $1B restoration; the adjoining half-acre Transamerica Redwood Park, a public grove of coast redwoods with a sculpture, is the free draw.
ph: Photo: TheWB · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: An 840-ft public promenade pier with antique iron lamp posts and wooden benches jutting into the bay; a favorite for anglers and photographers - the deck lines up straight at the Transamerica Pyramid.
ph: pier looking toward Yerba Buena Island
Photo: Michael Rowe · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: The West Coast's flagship modern-art museum, expanded by Snohetta into seven gallery floors with a free ground-floor Richard Serra and a living wall on the sculpture terrace. Open daily except Wednesday.
ph: Photo: Beyond My Ken · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: One of the largest Asian art collections in the West, 18,000+ works spanning 6,000 years, housed in the old Beaux-Arts main library on Civic Center. Open Thu-Mon; closed Tue/Wed.
Bayfront home of the SF Giants — the Coca-Cola bottle slide, the giant glove, McCovey Cove splash hits and the ballpark crab sandwich.
5.4-acre rooftop park atop the Salesforce Transit Center — 600 trees, 16,000 plants, a linear fountain, a gondola and ~20 free events a week.

rows.w: Beaux-Arts City Hall on Van Ness Avenue, the grand centrepiece of the Civic Center.

rows.w: The city's tallest building (1,070 ft, 2018), crowned by Jim Campbell's 'Day for Night' — a nine-story LED video sculpture of street scenes, surf and sky, visible nightly from up to 20 miles away. Pairs with Salesforce Park next door.
Three city blocks of gardens, public art and free concerts; walk behind the falling-water curtain of the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial.
Since 2005 a museum of the art and cultures of the African diaspora — steps from SFMOMA, with the striking photomosaic face wall.
Claes Oldenburg & Coosje van Bruggen's giant bow and arrow (2002) in Rincon Park on the Embarcadero — once maligned, now beloved as the spot where Tony Bennett 'left his heart'.

rows.n: Children's Creativity Museum & LeRoy King Carousel
rows.w: Hands-on animation, music and media studios for kids 2–12 atop Yerba Buena Gardens, with the jewel-studded 1906 LeRoy King Carousel out front.

The former federal penitentiary in the middle of the bay, now a Golden Gate NRA site with the audio-guided cellhouse tour, gardens and the 1969 occupation history; ferries depart Pier 33 Alcatraz Landing.
ph: Photo: Chris6d · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: North Beach's green heart under the twin spires of Saints Peter and Paul — morning tai chi, focaccia from the corner bakery. Free.
ph: Photo: Christopher Michel from San Francisco, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: Lawrence Halprin's 1982 plaza at the foot of Telegraph Hill — a granite water garden and a Sierra-inspired 'soft' park; the Chronicle calls it the best park along the Embarcadero, all but hidden from sight.
The 1898 Beaux-Arts ferry terminal with its landmark clock tower, reborn as a food hall of local artisans; the Tuesday/Thursday/Saturday farmers' market on the plaza is one of the country's best.

Beaux-Arts City Hall on Van Ness Avenue, the grand centrepiece of the Civic Center.
The 2.6-acre plaza at the heart of the shopping and hotel district, ringed by department stores. Free.
The 1875 Palace (rebuilt 1909 after the quake) — step into the Garden Court under 80,000 panes of stained glass.
ph: Photo: Original photograph by uploader Centpacrr · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: Foodwise's celebrated farmers market wrapping the Ferry Building — NorCal growers, bakers and street food; Tue & Thu 10–2, Sat 8–2 (Saturday is the big one).
Home of the San Francisco Symphony since it opened in 1980 — the Civic Center concert hall on Van Ness beside City Hall, the Opera House and SFJAZZ.
Willis Polk's 1918 seven-story wall of glass — believed to be the first American building with a glass curtain wall, and one of the city's most important architectural sights.
1875 cast-iron fountain where survivors of the 1906 earthquake used to meet — said to be haunted by them still. Free.
Greek Revival landmark (1874) that minted gold coins until 1937 — now used for exhibitions and events.
Michelin-starred, live-fire seafood from Saison Hospitality on the Embarcadero waterfront; embered oysters with smoked chili butter and a steak-knife radicchio salad, cooked over an open hearth.
Three Michelin stars — Corey Lee's modern Korean-American tasting room in SoMa.
Two Michelin stars (2026) — the SoMa hearth-cooking tasting room.
Two Michelin stars — Christopher Bleidorn's live-fire SoMa tasting room.
SF's oldest bar (1851) — built on the hull of the Gold Rush ship Arkansas, a Barbary Coast watering hole in Jackson Square.
Afternoon tea, popovers and one of SF's best burgers under the 1909 City of Paris stained-glass dome, overlooking Union Square.
SF's most historic French bistro (1974), heart of the 'French corridor' by Chinatown's Dragon Gate — revived by former staff; the cassoulet has a cult following.

First brick-and-mortar of a SF Jamaican caterer named for the owner's mother — flaky Jamaican beef patties at the Ferry Building; on SF Standard's 2026 cheap-eats panel and the Chronicle's hand-pie round-up.

Sorrel chef Alex Hong's 220-seat Californian, wood-fired flagship in the old Slanted Door space (Oct 2025) — the Infatuation says it single-handedly makes the Ferry Building worth going to; the Chronicle's critic found it surprisingly dull. On SF Standard's best-new-of-2025 list.

The city's definitive upscale Greek room in Jackson Square — open-hearth grill and wood oven perfuming a fireplace-lit dining room; grilled lamb chops, moussaka and some of the best grilled octopus in town.
Financial District grill dating to 1867 — curtained wooden booths, sand dabs and Hangtown fry; one of SF's handful of century-old dining rooms.
Since 1908 — the first downtown restaurant to reopen after the 1906 quake, where Sam Spade ate 'chops, baked potatoes, sliced tomatoes' in The Maltese Falcon.

rows: 3 places · kept for the record, newest check first

rows.n: Burlingame Museum of PEZ Memorabilia — CLOSED
rows.w: A beloved roadside oddity that displayed one of the world's largest PEZ dispenser collections plus banned/rare pieces and the 'world's largest PEZ dispenser.' Permanently closed in July 2019 - kept here for the record; do not visit.
Daniel Libeskind's tilted blue-steel cube grafted onto a 1907 power substation, one of downtown's boldest buildings.

Divisadero cafe milling its own whole-grain flour with Josey Baker Bread — the destination for SF's cult thick-cut sourdough toast. TEMPORARILY CLOSED after a June 29, 2026 fire; verify before visiting.
